paragraphs: Shares of French satellite operator Eutelsat rose 17.7% on Friday and were up 25% over five days, according to CNBC. The move followed a dispute over restrictions on Ukraine's military access to SpaceX's Starshield service.

Earlier this week, Kyiv accused SpaceX of imposing new restrictions on its military-grade Starlink service without warning, limiting connectivity and its ability to defend against Russian attacks. Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy said Starlink was "switched off" in the middle of the night, preventing drones from intercepting Russian attacks and contributing to civilian deaths. "They knew what they did," he said. SpaceX CEO Elon Musk responded that Starshield systems are under the control of Washington and President Donald Trump.

Deutsche Bank analysts said in a note on Thursday that the share move was more evidence "supporting the sovereign value of European Satellite networks," and that markets viewed Eutelsat as "the credible Starlink alternative." They also cautioned that Eutelsat lacks the scale to offer as many terminals as Starlink and said they would expect the shares to give up some of the gains.
The scale gap is large. Eutelsat, which consolidated with OneWeb in 2023, has over 600 satellites in orbit, while Starlink has more than 6,750, according to the companies' websites cited by CNBC.

Ukraine's deputy minister for recovery, infrastructure and transport, Serhiy Derkach, told CNBC that Russia had stepped up attacks on Ukrainian infrastructure, including bridges, railway networks and border crossings, taking advantage of the restrictions. He said Ukrainians already experience blackouts of 4 to 12 hours a day and that the country is heading toward "very harsh weeks and months." Whether the share gains hold is something investors will be watching.

Traders are betting heavily that the Federal Reserve will not raise interest rates at its Oct. 28 meeting, but CNBC's analysis argues that Chairman Kevin Warsh could still surprise. Futures markets assigned a 15% probability to an October hike as of Friday morning.

Speaking at an International Monetary Fund event in Bangkok, Warsh said he was not signaling a decision either way. He said that since September, "the world has broadly conformed to our expectations." CNBC read that as suggesting recent hot inflation data does not contradict the Fed's September projections, in which the median official expected one more hike in 2026, leaving room to pause in October and raise in December.

CNBC noted that Warsh has rejected the convention of telling markets his plans before meetings. At the September press conference he said of the committee's projections, "Those aren't my forecasts." Recent remarks by Vice Chairman Philip Jefferson and New York Fed President John Williams indicated little urgency to hike, and markets repriced toward a hold. CNBC said outsiders cannot be sure those officials still speak for the chair as they once did.

The inflation data gives a case for a hike, according to CNBC. The consumer price index rose 3.7% in the year through September and the producer price index rose 6.3%. CNBC said that implies core PCE inflation of about 3.1%. Warsh has called the Fed's 2% target "a firm, fixed target." He has also pointed to loose credit conditions and said the Fed had "removed a dose of accommodation."
CNBC concluded that how Warsh settles these questions is not yet clear, and that investors may be complacent. The press conference after the meeting should provide more answers.

Tesla showed its long-delayed next-generation Roadster on Thursday at a SpaceX test site in McGregor, Texas, according to CNBC. In a livestreamed demo, a white prototype raced up a curved ramp, clung to it upside down, vaulted off, flipped in mid-air and landed using SpaceX-derived technology. Tesla's timer showed zero to 60 miles per hour in under a second. Elon Musk said production would begin in 2028.

No price was announced, and it was unclear whether the car would be street-legal. Musk said, "This is not necessarily a safety-optimized car." Tesla has taken $50,000 deposits since 2017 and has missed every delivery target, CNBC reported. It also said the car is unlikely to have a material financial impact on the company.

The Verge was more critical, calling the demo pure spectacle. It said the "Rocket" version, which removes the passenger seat for gas tanks, will be invite-only and, per Tesla, not approved for public road use. The Verge also reported the range estimate was cut from 600 miles to 300 miles. It said the flying configuration will not become a production car that most buyers could own, and called the event a success only as a publicity stunt.

The unveiling added to speculation about a Tesla-SpaceX merger. CNBC said SpaceX went public in June and that its COO, Gwynne Shotwell, told CNBC a merger "might make Elon's life a little easier." Barclays analyst Dan Levy predicted in a note this week that a deal could come before the end of 2026. SpaceX is valued at about $2 trillion and Tesla at $1.4 trillion.
Tesla is scheduled to report third-quarter results after the bell on Wednesday.

Elon Musk gave $158 million to help the Senate Leadership Fund, the main Republican Senate super PAC, post the largest quarterly haul in its history, according to CNBC. A Federal Election Commission filing on Thursday showed the group raised $272.9 million from July through September and entered the final weeks before the Nov. 3 midterms with more than $155 million in cash.

CNBC said Musk's money came in September through an affiliated Texas PAC created to support Republican Ken Paxton, in two contributions of $75 million and $83 million. His giving alone exceeded the Democratic Senate Majority PAC's third-quarter total of $151 million. That group reported $111.8 million in cash, though its FEC filings were not yet available.

The money arrives as Republicans defend a 53-seat Senate majority. CNBC reported the fund paused advertising in North Carolina after spending more than $30 million and shifted resources to Kansas, where Sen. Roger Marshall faces Democrat Adam Hamilton. It also committed $15 million in Nebraska to defend Sen. Pete Ricketts. In Texas, Democrat James Talarico has made a once-safe Republican race one of the most expensive in the country. Republican groups spent about $122 million there in September, according to AdImpact data. Talarico said he raised $64 million in the third quarter, while Paxton raised $10.2 million.

Wired reported that Musk's America PAC also spent $76.7 million in the third quarter, including $35.8 million on a field operation to turn out Trump's base in all seven Senate battleground states and some House races. Wired said the effort rivals his 2024 operation and makes him the largest known donor of the midterms across both parties.
America PAC had more than $12 million left, Wired said, and Musk may contribute more.

Gaza's Health Ministry said on Friday that malnutrition and starvation rates in the Strip have reached "catastrophic" levels. It released the statement for World Food Day, according to Al Jazeera, and said the situation persists despite a US-brokered ceasefire meant in part to let more food and medical supplies in.

The ministry said at least 466 Palestinians have died of malnutrition and starvation since 2024, and that children account for one-third of those deaths. Elderly Palestinians accounted for the largest share, with 189 deaths, or 40.5 percent. The ministry said 11 percent of older people went without a meal for an entire day and 48 percent reduced portions so their families could eat. It estimated that 74,200 children would need treatment for acute malnutrition through April 2027. It also said anaemia among pregnant women has risen to 61 percent in 2026, from 41 percent before the war began in October 2023, and that nearly 4,000 pregnancy losses were recorded in the first half of 2026.
The ministry warned that more than 1.4 million people, or 67 percent of Gaza's population, are projected to face crisis-level food insecurity or worse through the end of 2026 as winter approaches.

UNICEF published a report on Friday saying gains in tackling the hunger crisis are fragile. It said a scaled-up food and nutrition response and eased restrictions on supplies helped avert a prolonged famine after one was declared in August 2025. UNICEF spokesperson Ricardo Pires said commercial and humanitarian supplies must remain predictable and continuous.

Israel said on Wednesday that no commercial goods had entered Gaza in days and blamed a tax dispute between local merchants and Hamas. Hamas called the claim "baseless", and Gaza's Government Media Office called it a disinformation campaign. The Health Ministry called for international action to ensure unrestricted entry of food and medicine and for support to revive local food production.

Irish novelist Sally Rooney's books will no longer be sold in the UK, after her publisher said current legislation prevents it from passing UK earnings on to her. Faber said in a statement that selling a writer's work without being able to pay her is "an unconscionable situation" and that it made the decision "in full agreement with Sally".

The issue stems from Rooney's announcement last year that she would donate proceeds from her books to Palestine Action, which the UK banned under terrorism legislation in July last year. Under UK law, anyone providing financial assistance to the group could face up to 14 years in prison. Rooney has said she believes Israel is committing genocide in Gaza, an allegation Israel vehemently denies. She told NPR she is "wholly prepared to accept the consequences".

The British government said it banned the group over serious damage to property and said its methods had become more aggressive. Critics, including UN human rights chief Volker Türk and Amnesty International UK, have questioned the ban on free speech grounds. According to the Guardian, 419 writers have signed an open letter backing Rooney.

The Guardian also reported that national security adviser Jonathan Powell is under pressure over a post on X by his wife, author Sarah Helm, backing Palestine Action authors. Police said the post is being assessed. Downing Street said Helm's views are held by an individual who does not represent the government. The Campaign Against Antisemitism called for her to face the law, while the group Defend Our Juries thanked her for defying the ban.
The ban has been challenged in court: the High Court ruled against it in February, an appeal court overturned that, and the case goes to Britain's highest court next month.

Brazilian President Luiz Inácio Lula da Silva said in a Thursday night TV Globo interview that he now supports lowering the age of criminal responsibility from 18 to 16 for "heinous" crimes. The Guardian described the move as a reversal of a longstanding position held by Lula and his party, coming just over a week before the October 25 run-off.

Lula said he took the view after polls showed 80 percent of the population supports lowering the age. Flávio Bolsonaro, his opponent, and his father, former president Jair Bolsonaro, have long backed lowering it, to 14. Brazilian law lists many crimes as heinous, from murder and rape to drug trafficking, the offence for which about a quarter of the 816,000 people serving sentences are held. Human rights groups and security experts have criticised such proposals, arguing they do little against violence and increase recruitment into organised crime. The Episcopal Conference of Brazil also criticised the proposal in the Senate.

Al Jazeera reported that a CNT/MDA poll released Friday put Flávio Bolsonaro at 46.8 percent and Lula at 45.9 percent. Quaest had Bolsonaro at 46 percent to Lula's 44, and Datafolha had 47 to 45. All three fall within a 2 percent margin of error, so many experts still consider the race a toss-up.

Bolsonaro led the October 4 first round by about 2.2 million votes. Lula has since secured congressional approval for a shorter working week, debt relief for microentrepreneurs and a promise of free weekend public transport, according to the Guardian. Bolsonaro, who has pledged a crackdown on crime, also ended up backing the shorter working week.

Prime Minister Mark Carney urged Albertans to vote to stay in Canada at a rally in Calgary on Thursday, ahead of Monday's independence referendum. The BBC reported that he warned the "stakes are high" and said the vote is happening "at the worst possible time". He asked for a "decisive result" against separation.

Carney told a crowd of more than 7,000 that "turnout will determine the outcome", cautioning against relying on polls, which indicate most Albertans support a united Canada. More than 450,000 people have already voted early or by mail, and the average number of ballots cast so far is higher than in Alberta's last provincial general election. The question asks whether Albertans want to remain in Canada or start the process of holding a binding separation referendum.

Premier Danielle Smith called the referendum after a grassroots group gathered around 300,000 petition signatures. Smith has advocated staying in Canada but has described the vote as a chance to hear from Albertans. Separation supporters argue Alberta has been overlooked by Ottawa and would keep more of its wealth. Opponents say an independent Alberta would inherit billions in debt and lose jobs and investment.

Carney acknowledged that Albertans' frustrations "are real" and pointed to his plan to fast-track a new oil pipeline to the Pacific coast. The ballot also has nine other questions, many on immigration control. Carney urged people to "vote no to the nine", while Smith supports them. Smith replied on X that they have common ground but said he misunderstands the effect of Liberal immigration policy on costs.
Smith and Conservative leader Pierre Poilievre are due at a unity event in Calgary on Friday. Carney speaks in Edmonton, where separatists plan a rally Saturday.

Protesters and anti-riot police have clashed in several Albanian cities this week, the BBC reports, in scenes it describes as not witnessed for decades. Government buildings and some private businesses have been attacked. Clashes began Tuesday in Tirana and spread to Durrës, Shkodër, Lezhë, Vlora, Gjirokastër and Korçë.

The new demonstrations were announced as a student movement about education costs and the cost of living, and secondary school pupils joined. Masked protesters threw stones, and police responded with water cannon, tear gas and batons. A floor of the education ministry was set on fire. Dozens of police have been hurt. The BBC said street violence remains contained for now, and the UK government has advised visitors to avoid demonstrations.

The unrest follows months of protest by the anti-government "Flamingo" movement, which began over a tourism project linked to Jared Kushner on the Adriatic coast. For about 135 evenings, protesters called for Prime Minister Edi Rama to resign. Allegations of corruption among officials have grown: one deputy prime minister has fled the country and another was ordered to step down. Young protesters told the BBC the current phase was born from peaceful protests that were met with "humiliation, ridicule, mockery". The BBC says an overlap is possible but no leaders have confirmed it.

Rama has ruled out resigning and promised to "listen, address legitimate concerns". He blamed opposition leader Sali Berisha for instigating chaos, and also spoke of "foreign hands" without naming anyone. The BBC noted Berisha's Democratic Party has drawn smaller crowds than the current protests, and described allegations against Serbia as unfounded. Berisha's response was not included in the report.

Pope Leo XIV plans to appear before the public on Sunday, his first appearance since lung surgery on Tuesday, the Vatican said. He will deliver the traditional noontime prayer. His doctors said on Friday that he can "carry out normal daily activities with full independence" and that a blood test and chest X-ray showed "steady improvement".

The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed at Rome's Gemelli Hospital. The Vatican said the whole lobe was taken "to ensure the procedure was radical" and that the operation was successful and free of complications. He was diagnosed with lung adenocarcinoma. On Sunday he had told the crowd in St Peter's Square that doctors had found a "well-contained" nodule at an early stage.

The Vatican released the first images since the surgery, showing Leo celebrating Mass on the hospital's tenth floor and standing unaided. It did not say when he will be discharged, though it previously indicated recovery would take about a week. Doctors have not disclosed the tumour's size or whether the disease reached nearby lymph nodes, factors that help determine prognosis.
Cardinal Blase Cupich, seen as a close ally, told America magazine he thought Leo had "downplayed" the issue and found the malignancy "more shocking and more concerning".

Leo is due to visit Uruguay, Argentina and Peru from November 6 to 17. Peru's president had speculated the trip might be delayed, but the Vatican said work on it is "going forward" and released a list of journalists admitted to cover it. On Friday Leo also spoke by phone with Russian President Vladimir Putin, pressing for a ceasefire to allow aid into the occupied Ukrainian town of Oleshky, the Vatican said.

Director of National Intelligence Jay Clayton said on CNBC's "Squawk Box" Friday that US companies and the Trump administration "need to be wary" of foreign espionage as the race for artificial intelligence dominance continues. He cited a recently revealed case involving OpenAI as an example.

Saudi national Abdulrahman Alfozan, a former OpenAI employee, is charged with allegedly installing a recording device in an executive conference room at the company. CNBC noted he has not been charged with espionage; the federal charge involves alleged interception of oral communications. According to federal prosecutors, he had booked a one-way ticket to Saudi Arabia with his wife and another family member before his arrest. An ex-CIA official, speaking anonymously, told CNBC the case is "probably the tip of the iceberg."

Clayton said both commercial and state-sponsored espionage "are realities" and that the case shows "the lengths that people will go to try and supplant our leadership" in AI. He said AI "amplifies" existing cybersecurity risks to digital infrastructure tied to public goods, national defense and global communications, which is why the government is focused on hardening those systems.

Clayton, appointed AI czar earlier this month, leads a new White House AI task force that held its first meeting Thursday. He said it built on an accord signed last month by President Trump and AI leaders, which includes industry pledges to police AI risks and which Trump called "morally binding". The task force set up three subcommittees: reporting and response, critical infrastructure, and law enforcement and responsibility.
Clayton said China, Russia, Iran and North Korea all have significant technical capability and that the US needs to stay ahead of them.

Meta's updated commercial terms, effective October 30, appear to let the company crawl websites "associated" with businesses that use its platforms, including news publishers, according to Nieman Lab as reported by The Verge and Ars Technica. The terms say Meta may use content from those sites to "develop, improve, research" and "train" its products.

The terms apply to business accounts across Facebook, Instagram, WhatsApp and Messenger. They authorize Meta to use scrapers, bots and crawlers, and to create test credentials, to access content tied to a business's products or services. Businesses that disagree "may stop all access or use" of Meta products for commercial purposes, the terms say. Ars Technica reported there is no opt-out, and that the word AI does not appear, with the meaning inferred from the word "train".

Meta says it is only consolidating terms. Spokesperson Daniel Roberts said there is "no change to how Meta uses web crawlers" and that content owners can still use robots.txt. Communications chief Andy Stone said the update is meant to pull accurate product information for ads, not to scrape news sites. Ars Technica said Meta pointed to a Seller Agreement as precedent for the test credentials language, but found the new terms use fresh and broader wording.

Legal experts told Nieman Lab it is unclear whether a court would enforce the terms, but that Meta could use them to argue they supersede robots.txt blocks. Cornell professor James Grimmelmann said the terms could permit Meta to train AI on any content from publishers' sites and possibly use it in competition with them. Attorney Matt Topic called it a remarkable provision to bury in terms of service.
Nieman Lab also noted Meta recently began charging businesses and creators to include links in posts.

Sen. Susan Collins, a Maine Republican, and Democratic challenger Troy Jackson clashed over billionaire donors, party loyalty and working-class voters Thursday night in their fourth debate. Fox News described the exchange as taking a notably personal turn.

Collins questioned whether Jackson had kept his promise to reject billionaire donors, citing FEC contribution records. Jackson acknowledged that "the billionaires that I might have on my campaign, that is accurate." He said he had not made deals with billionaires the way Collins has, and that he would tax them if elected. Fox noted that Jackson did not specify what agreements he meant.

On independence from President Trump, Collins cited her opposition to Pete Hegseth's confirmation as defense secretary. She said she organized votes against him and that one Republican changed his mind at the last minute. Jackson answered that Hegseth was confirmed anyway, and said that whenever Trump needs her, Collins is there. Collins called herself the most bipartisan member of the Senate. She disputed Jackson's claim that she votes with Trump 92 or 94 percent of the time, saying that figure covers only a third of votes and that across 90 percent of votes it is 72 percent. Jackson said he is no rubber stamp, noting that Democratic Gov. Janet Mills vetoed 40 of his bills.

A heckler interrupted the debate, and Collins called him "obviously one of Troy's supporters." Jackson replied, "Oh shut up. I don't even know that kid." Near the end, Jackson, a former logger, asked whether Collins looks down on him or on working-class people generally. Collins said she does not, noting that she grew up in Caribou, picked potatoes as her first job and has worked since age ten.
Maine's general election is Nov. 3, with control of the U.S. Senate at stake.

The Trump administration sued California election officials on Thursday, arguing they did not act quickly enough to review names the federal government identified as "likely" noncitizens. According to Fox News, the Justice Department asked a judge to block the state from counting mail-in ballots from those individuals unless their eligibility can be confirmed.

The Justice Department's complaint says U.S. Citizenship and Immigration Services conducted a "multiagency and multilevel review" and determined with "high confidence" that roughly 20,000 people on California's voter rolls were likely noncitizens. The California secretary of state's office said it was given only 48 hours to review the names and that the federal government had not provided the underlying evidence or methodology.

Fox also reported that the president has repeatedly argued noncitizen voting is a serious threat to election integrity, while studies and prosecutions have found documented instances of noncitizens casting ballots to be rare. It noted that federal courts have repeatedly rejected administration efforts to compel states to turn over voter information.

Separately, the League of Women Voters, the Electronic Privacy Information Center and the League of United Latin American Citizens filed a complaint in federal court in Washington, D.C. It alleges the Department of Homeland Security has obtained voter files from at least 47 states and handled the data in violation of federal law, including a policy to combine it with commercial datasets. The suit says officials in 30 states had previously refused federal demands for voter information. It asks the court to declare the collection illegal, block the policy and order DHS to delete the data. DHS did not immediately respond to Fox's request for comment.
Both cases come less than three weeks before Election Day.

Lawyers for the Trump administration are scheduled to argue Friday before a three-judge panel of the U.S. Court of Appeals for the D.C. Circuit that papers created in the White House belong to Donald Trump rather than the American people. NPR reports the case could end up at the conservative-leaning Supreme Court.

For about 200 years, presidents could decide for themselves what to do with the papers they created in office. After disputes with Richard Nixon, Congress passed the Presidential Records Act, in place since 1978. NPR says every president followed it until this year. Six months ago, the Justice Department moved to invalidate the law. White House spokeswoman Lauren Bis said the act is unconstitutional and violates the separation of powers. The administration has also argued in court papers that keeping all the records burdens the White House and could chill advisers from speaking candidly to the president.

NPR notes the shift came after Trump was indicted on obstruction charges over classified documents at Mar-a-Lago. A judge dismissed that case on technical grounds, and the Justice Department dropped it after his reelection.

Citizens for Responsibility and Ethics in Washington, a watchdog group, sued. Its chief counsel, Nikhel Sus, said a win for the administration would mean the public has no right of access to presidential papers. Senior U.S. District Judge John Bates ruled against the White House this year.

Conservative lawyer Michael Edney said parts of the act that give Congress automatic access and presume public disclosure are "constitutionally problematic," and he doubted the watchdog groups have standing. He said the administration wants the case at the Supreme Court on its own timing. Former Bush official John Bellinger said access to past presidents' records is vital for continuity of government.

A 16-year-old broke into Silver Rail Elementary School in Bend, Oregon, on Thursday and killed three children, ages 5, 8 and 11, and a teacher, officials said. A 7-year-old and a 54-year-old were hospitalized. A bystander shot the suspect after following him into the school, according to local officials.

Bend Police Chief Mike Krantz said the first emergency call came at 12:59 p.m. from a person in a vehicle who reported being shot at by someone carrying a long gun. Officers arrived within three minutes, and soon afterward an officer reported that a community member had shot the teenager. Police said the suspect entered by firing at locked doors, and that they did not know whether he knew anyone at the school or had attended it. NPR noted that the district's website describes secure sign-in vestibules, visitor ID checks and buzz-in systems. The Associated Press, cited by Fox News, reported that the shooter used his mother's shotgun.

Several Democrats renewed calls for gun control. Sen. Ron Wyden called for common-sense gun laws. Sen. Martin Heinrich said the measures Congress passed after Uvalde did not go far enough. Sen. Elizabeth Warren said Congress must do much more and cited more than 50 school shootings this year. Statements from Sen. Jeff Merkley and Gov. Tina Kotek stopped short of calling for new regulation. Fox did not report responses from Republican lawmakers.

The school serves kindergarten through fifth grade and has 467 students. The Bend-La Pine district canceled classes and activities at all 32 of its schools on Friday. Authorities are still working to piece together how the attack unfolded and how the teenager obtained the weapon.

President Trump announced Thursday that the planned execution of Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan will not be livestreamed. "He will die, as scheduled, by firing squad, but this event will not be streamed," Trump wrote on Truth Social. Fox News reports that Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth had announced earlier this month that the Dec. 3 execution would be publicly viewable. Trump said family members of the victims will be allowed to attend in person.

Hasan, a former Army psychiatrist, killed 13 people and wounded 32 in the 2009 attack in Texas. He was sentenced to death in a 2013 military trial. NPR says appeals could delay the execution, which would be the military's first firing squad execution since World War II.

NPR cited an October ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos poll in which 52 percent of Americans support Hasan's execution, but 80 percent say it should not be livestreamed. One U.S. official, speaking to NPR anonymously, said Trump was talked out of a livestream because it was against American values and because of concern the footage could appear on jihadi websites and endanger U.S. forces. Fox spoke with several Americans, most of whom welcomed the reversal. Some said it was meant to protect Trump's image, and one said he would have watched.

More broadly, NPR reports that about two-thirds of Americans support the death penalty for murder, according to a Pew poll from this summer, while Gallup's 2025 figure of 52 percent is the lowest in more than 50 years. Emory historian Daniel LaChance said support is "a mile wide and an inch deep," because when polls offer life without parole, 60 percent prefer it. Six states carried out the 31 executions this year.

U.S. health officials are moving ahead with a plan to let specialty pharmacies produce certain peptides, a class of largely unregulated injections popular among followers of Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and other wellness influencers, according to the Associated Press report published by STAT.

The Department of Health and Human Services sent a peptides "interim access policy" to the White House Office of Management and Budget for review, according to a Thursday posting on a government website. The filing gives no specifics. Two people familiar with the plan, speaking anonymously, said it would let pharmacies temporarily compound some of the most popular peptides, including BPC-157, which is promoted to build muscle and heal injuries. HHS did not immediately respond to requests for comment.

The approach, known as enforcement discretion, would assure compounding pharmacies they will not be targeted for making certain peptides. Formally adding them to the FDA's list of drugs safe for compounding would require rulemaking that could take years, and it was unclear whether the administration still plans to pursue it.

The FDA had previously placed BPC-157 and more than a dozen other injectable peptides on its list of substances too risky to compound, citing possible contamination, allergic reactions and tumor growth. The uses are not FDA-approved, and most data comes from animal studies. In July, an outside advisory panel chosen by Kennedy's department recommended dropping restrictions on six of seven peptides considered, against the conclusions of FDA staff scientists, who said none had been studied enough to establish safety and effectiveness.

Kennedy has said compounding pharmacies must be allowed to sell peptides because Americans are turning to gray-market products from China and elsewhere. Telehealth firms Hims & Hers and Noom plan to offer peptides if access is eased, and analysts estimate the market at $2 billion to $3 billion.

Police in New Delhi detained Abhijeet Dipke, leader of the youth "Cockroach" movement, on Friday ahead of a demonstration he had called in the Connaught Place district. NPR and The Guardian both reported that thousands gathered anyway, with The Guardian putting the crowd at about 2,000, waving Indian flags and demanding the resignation of chief election commissioner Gyanesh Kumar.

The protests center on a review of voter lists that has removed more than 130 million names since last year. Critics say the exercise is politically motivated, risks disenfranchising millions and has disproportionately affected minorities, particularly Muslims. The Election Commission and Prime Minister Narendra Modi's government deny that, saying the revision removes duplicate and ineligible entries.

The Guardian reported that Dipke called the protest after two fellow leaders, Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka, were jailed for five days for jumping police barricades and briefly waving the flag at a restricted site. Police sent Dipke a notice to cancel, and the local authority closed the park. Student leader Neha Bora was also detained. Dipke said, "Waving the tricolor is not a crime." The Guardian described the authorities' response as a draconian crackdown, including gathering bans and thousands of detentions last weekend.

Modi has not commented publicly. NPR reported that some party leaders have called the demonstrators "anarchists" and suggested, without evidence, foreign backing. BJP spokesperson Sambit Patra said the protesters' intent is to stage a coup, according to The Guardian.

The movement began as online satire after India's chief justice compared unemployed young people to parasites, and protests forced the education minister's resignation in July. NPR said it is unclear whether the protests will grow into a wider political movement, since Modi's government remains electorally strong.

Masked Israeli settlers attacked Palestinians harvesting olives across the occupied West Bank on Friday, injuring several people including Washington Post photographer Heidi Levine, according to NPR and The Guardian. The Palestinian Red Crescent Society said about two dozen attacks left 20 people injured.

Levine, who the Post said was wearing a vest marked "press," said from a hospital that she saw at least 50 masked men with slingshots on a hilltop and was pushed to the ground and repeatedly kicked. The Guardian reported that witnesses said the attack lasted more than 10 minutes and that her passport, phone, wallet and equipment were taken. She said Palestinian colleagues intervened. Post executive editor Matt Murray called it an unwarranted attack and urged a thorough investigation. Israeli police said they would investigate and bring those involved to justice. The U.S. Embassy said it condemns criminal violence by any party.

Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu's office said the facts were "unclear," blamed "200 Arabs and far-left activists" who confronted Israeli youths, and said it condemns violence against anyone. The Israeli Foreign Press Association said its repeated calls for action have been ignored.

The Guardian reported that in Abu Falah, at least 80 settlers gathered in view of Israeli military vehicles, and that troops fired teargas toward Palestinians who picked up rocks. Yesh Din counts at least 170 settler attacks since Sept. 27. Palestinian authorities say at least four Palestinians have been killed and more than 100 injured in the past month.

The Guardian also reported that new military rules bar Palestinians from about 8,800 hectares of Area C farmland without approval, up 30 percent from last year. Sara Qudah of the Committee to Protect Journalists called the attack part of a pattern of violence against journalists.

Japan's Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) spacecraft is set to launch from the Tanegashima Space Center with the aim of bringing back a sample from Phobos, the larger of Mars's two moons. NASA lists the launch target as 3:41 p.m. EDT on Monday, Oct. 19, which is 4:41 a.m. in Japan on Tuesday, Oct. 20.

According to New Scientist, the spacecraft should reach Mars in August 2027 and enter an orbit alongside Phobos to map its surface. It will also observe Deimos. Operators at the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) will then pick a landing spot. During one or two brief landings, MMX will drop off a small rover called IDEFIX and collect samples. New Scientist says the rover is the first placed on such a small body, so part of its job is to confirm that a wheeled rover works in very low gravity.

Two devices will gather the samples. One uses a puff of gas to blow dust and pebbles into a container. The other drives a hollow cylinder several centimeters into the ground. NASA says sample collection will come no earlier than December 2028, with delivery to Earth in 2031.

Researchers have long debated whether the moons are captured asteroids or formed from an impact on Mars. New Scientist notes that their shapes and surfaces resemble asteroids, while their circular orbits around Mars's equator fit the impact idea better. NASA's Tom Statler said the answer would help illuminate the early era when the inner planets may have been acquiring water and organic compounds.

NASA is contributing the MEGANE spectrograph, the pneumatic sampler, Deep Space Network support and funding for U.S. scientists. It will curate about 15 percent of the returned sample at Johnson Space Center in Houston. NASA's Nicky Fox said the samples will bring "paradigm-shifting science" on the Mars system.

Blue Origin said Friday that it plans extensive upgrades to its Florida launch facilities, with the goal of supporting multiple flights per week by the end of the decade. The company will add two more launch and landing pads for New Glenn, its heavy-lift, partially reusable rocket, according to CNBC.

A $330 million expansion of its Rocket Park campus in Cape Canaveral is expected to be finished in the summer of 2027. Blue Origin said in a blog post that it will let the company produce up to 150 New Glenn upper stages a year. It is also building a new customer integration facility with the U.S. Space Force at Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, which would let it prepare multiple missions at once. Ian Richardson, the company's senior vice president of operations, wrote that the investments aim at "more missions, more reliably, and more efficiently."
Richardson said Blue Origin has invested more than $3 billion in its Florida infrastructure, which spans more than 20 sites in Brevard and Orange counties and employs more than 5,000 people.

The expansion comes as the company tries to compete with SpaceX for commercial and government customers. Blue Origin is also recovering from a May setback, when a New Glenn rocket exploded on the launchpad. CNBC reports the company is restoring the pad with a goal of returning New Glenn to flight by the end of 2026.

CNBC also reported that CEO Dave Limp said last month that the company's first outside funding round was oversubscribed. The Wall Street Journal reported that it raised $10 billion at a $140 billion valuation. CNBC adds that SpaceX has stopped offering commercial rides on Falcon 9 to prioritize Starship, contributing to a launch capacity shortage.

Representatives from 69 countries voted on Oct. 15 to abolish leap seconds, according to New Scientist. The vote took place at a meeting of the International Bureau of Weights and Measures (BIPM) in Versailles, France. Under the change, universal time will be allowed to drift up to an hour from astronomical time before being corrected. The change takes effect on May 20, 2027.

Leap seconds have been added to coordinated universal time 27 times since 1972. They were needed because natural fluctuations in Earth's rotation meant atomic time drifted from the sky. Supporters of ending them point to how much more technological systems now rely on precise timekeeping, from stock markets to telecommunications to GPS. Setnam Shemar of the UK's National Physical Laboratory said past leap seconds have crashed websites and disrupted airline booking systems.

Another concern is that Earth's rotation has recently begun to accelerate slightly. That raises the possibility of a first-ever negative leap second, whose consequences are hard to predict, said Noël Dimarcq, who heads the BIPM's committee on time and frequency. He said the new approach should give an uninterrupted flow of time for several centuries.

Emily Akkermans of the Royal Observatory in Greenwich said the growing gap will eventually be like living on daylight saving time permanently. Shemar stressed that the effects are small, saying it will be many hundreds or even thousands of years before a leap hour is needed. Physicists will keep tracking Earth's rotation for astronomy and celestial navigation.

The meeting also asked for proposals on a new definition of the second, because optical clocks are now more accurate than the caesium clock used today. It also called on international agencies to consider a universal time standard for the moon.

Hundreds of children have died of starvation and disease in a drought in Sudan linked to this year's El Niño, New Scientist reports. The Integrated Food Security Phase Classification (IPC), a partnership of the United Nations and charity organisations, said almost half the country is in drought, in some areas the worst in decades. It described a "humanitarian catastrophe, already of historic proportions."

Hunger has reached famine levels in two refugee camps in Darfur, though not enough for the IPC to declare a famine across the region. Almost 29 million people, 62 percent of the population, are eating less or going hungry. Manon Radosta of the charity CARE said that after a poor harvest, families will be unable to store food or earn money before the rains in June, and that she is "extremely worried" about mass starvation.

Other pressures compound the drought. The civil war has displaced 14 million people and disrupted farming. Food and fuel prices have risen as the US-Iran conflict interrupts shipping through the Strait of Hormuz. Ninety percent of Sudan's agriculture depends on rain. Donor countries have given $1.25 billion of the $2.87 billion in aid the UN says is needed this year.

NASA, meanwhile, says satellites are tracking El Niño. It cites NOAA as giving an 83 percent chance that the strongest El Niño since 1950 is unfolding. NASA says eastern Pacific sea surface temperatures are about 3 degrees Fahrenheit above average and could rise a little more.

New Scientist says forecasters expect further warming, a likely hottest year on record in 2027, and possible heatwaves across the tropics next spring. Liz Stephens of the University of Reading warned of extreme heat across the Sahel next year.

Bulgaria has formally asked NATO to deploy combat aircraft and anti-drone systems, Defence Minister Dimitar Stoyanov said on Friday. The request follows a series of drone attacks on commercial shipping in the Black Sea, according to Defense News.

Drones hit two ships that caught fire off Romania's Black Sea coast this week. On Tuesday, a commercial vessel sank off Bulgaria's coast after a drone attack, and Sofia summoned Russia's ambassador. The article says the attacks highlight the growing threat that drone warfare linked to the Russia-Ukraine conflict poses to shipping near NATO's southeastern flank.

Stoyanov said Bulgaria has sent letters to the NATO Secretary General and the Supreme Allied Commander urging them to strengthen its capabilities, which also means deploying additional forces on Bulgarian territory. "We are awaiting their decision," he said. He added that he plans to meet his Romanian and Turkish counterparts soon to discuss coordinated action and a common approach to the Black Sea situation.

NATO Secretary General Mark Rutte met Bulgarian Prime Minister Rumen Radev and Romanian President Nicusor Dan on Thursday. Afterward he said NATO would keep working closely with Allies in the Black Sea, "adjusting our deterrence and defence posture as needed." Asked about Bulgaria's request, a NATO official said ambassadors from the alliance's 32 member states would discuss it further next week.

Bulgaria has also proposed a moratorium on attacks on civilian ships in the Black Sea. It expects to join a NATO anti-drone initiative by the end of October. Russia's response to the summoning of its ambassador was not reported in the article.

German police have detained a 28-year-old Russian man accused of being part of a cyber-crime gang that caused chaos at London hospitals and contributed to a patient's death, the BBC reports. German press named him as Vladimir K. The BBC says German detectives are now including the 2024 attack on blood testing company Synnovis in their investigation.

According to German officials, he was arrested by Japanese police in May when he arrived for a holiday. He is accused of being a core member of the Qilin gang, which has allegedly hacked more than 4,000 organisations since 2024 and extorted more than $140 million. He was wanted in Germany over a September 2024 hack of a logistics company, in which data was encrypted and about $160,000 in cryptocurrency demanded. His extradition was first reported in early October.

Qilin targeted Synnovis on June 3, 2024. A critical incident was declared at some London hospitals, with blood transfusion services severely disrupted, operations cancelled and emergency patients diverted. In total, the BBC says, more than 10,000 appointments were disrupted. King's College Hospital NHS Foundation Trust confirmed a year later that one patient had "died unexpectedly", with a long wait for a blood test result among several contributing factors. The BBC describes this as the first cyber attack directly linked to a death.

Separately, the BBC has learned that British police are examining whether its own inquiry may lead to an unlawful killing case, potentially a world first for cyber-crime. A 2020 negligent homicide investigation in Düsseldorf was dropped after experts concluded the patient would have died regardless and prosecutors could not prove the attack was the direct cause.
The BBC notes that hackers are rarely arrested in Russia, whose government refuses to cooperate with Western law enforcement requests.

Stryker said this week it has invested about $400 million in CMR Surgical, the Cambridge, U.K.-based maker of the Versius surgical robot, according to The Robot Report. The deal includes an exclusive option for Stryker to acquire CMR's remaining equity, and an exclusive U.S. commercial agency agreement for the Versius portfolio.

Under the arrangement, Stryker will be the exclusive U.S. sales agent for Versius. CMR will keep leading portfolio development and commercialization outside the United States. The option would let Stryker buy 100 percent of CMR's outstanding equity in the future, subject to the agreement's terms. The transaction needs regulatory approvals and must meet customary closing conditions. Stryker's Andy Pierce will also join CMR's board.

CMR CEO Massimiliano Colella called the alliance a strong endorsement of the company's technology and said the investment would help accelerate innovation and global expansion. Pierce, Stryker's group president of medsurg and neurotechnology, described soft-tissue robotics as a high-growth adjacency and a natural extension of Stryker's strengths in endoscopy and visualization. He said the company had evaluated the segment for years and called this a "thoughtful and disciplined entry."

CMR says Versius supports procedures including general, colorectal, urology, gynecology and thoracic surgery. It says the system is used in hospitals in more than 30 countries and has been used in 45,000 cases. The company said its modular design is meant to give flexibility across procedures and sites of care. Those descriptions come from CMR.
In the U.S., the Versius Plus system has FDA 510(k) clearance for cholecystectomy, and CMR has filed a 510(k) submission for benign gynecological indications.
